title: Relative hybridization textures as local coordinates for band geometry and topology
authors: Caiyuan Ye, Zhong Fang, Hongming Weng, Quansheng Wu
abstract: Global diagnostics such as Berry curvature and quantum metrics characterize the geometry and topology of an occupied Bloch subspace, leaving the microscopic sectors that carry this structure implicit. We introduce the relative hybridization coordinate $Z$ as a projector-level diagnostic connecting these global quantities to local degrees of freedom. As the Grassmann graph coordinate relative to a chosen sector, $Z$ reconstructs the local projector and retains the phase and matrix orientation absent from ordinary weight or fat-band descriptions. On valid chart patches, its momentum-space texture encodes Berry curvature, quantum metric, Berry phases, and Wilson loops, while chart obstructions appear as rank-drop defects whose balanced-chart winding of $\det Z$ gives the first Chern number. In the QWZ model this defect inventory reproduces the Chern phase diagram. In the lattice BHZ model, matrix $Z$ diagnoses the orbital $E|H$ partition as a robust matched chart for the QSH geometry, while the spin partition remains essential to the block and $\mathbb Z_2$ interpretation and shows rank deficiency as a matched chart in the spin-conserving limit. The relative hybridization coordinate thus provides a sector-resolved framework for relating band geometry and topology to microscopic structure.
summary: This work introduces the relative hybridization coordinate $Z$ as a powerful diagnostic tool to bridge the gap between abstract global topological invariants and concrete, sector-specific microscopic details of electronic bands. By analyzing the momentum-space texture of $Z$, researchers can robustly calculate quantities like the Chern number while explicitly tracking which physical components (e.g., orbital or spin sectors) contribute to the observed topology.
main_problem: Global topological diagnostics (like Berry curvature) characterize band geometry but fail to specify the underlying microscopic sectors responsible for these invariants.
main_result: The relative hybridization coordinate $Z$ provides a sector-resolved framework that connects global topology and geometry directly to local, microscopic degrees of freedom within the occupied Bloch subspace.
method: The authors introduce $Z$, defined as a projector-level diagnostic (Grassmann graph coordinate) relating the occupied subspace to chosen reference sectors ($A$ vs. $B$). Topological invariants are then read from defects in the momentum-space texture of $Z$.
model_or_system: The framework is applied generally to Bloch subspaces in condensed matter systems, with specific tests on the Qi-Wu-Zhang (QWZ) Chern insulator and the lattice BHZ model.
key_observables: Relative hybridization coordinate $Z$, quantum geometric tensors ($T_{ij}$), chart viability field ($\sigma_{\min}(P_{AA})$), and topological invariants like the first Chern number derived from defect winding.
important_parameters: The dimension matching between sectors ($	ext{dim } A$ vs. $N_{	ext{occ}}$) is crucial for defining the coordinate $Z$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on fixing a microscopic partition of the Hilbert space ($H = A \oplus B$) and assuming the existence of open patches where key projections are invertible.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates that the magnitude of $Z$ measures local mixing strength, while its phase retains coherent information about sector-resolved hybridization.
paper_structure: The paper develops the mathematical formalism for $Z$, derives geometric tensors from it, and then applies this machinery to calculate known topological invariants (Chern number via defect counting) in benchmark models like QWZ and BHZ.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state topology, the concept of using a local coordinate system ($Z$) derived from projection operators to diagnose global properties is highly relevant for characterizing entanglement structures or effective Hamiltonians in open quantum systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Physical motivation for the relative hybridization texture. Local degrees of freedom coupled by hopping and hybridization generate momentum-dependent band embed- dings. A conventional band plot shows the dispersion, while a partition into reference and complementary sectors resolves how the occupied states are completed from one sector into the other. The relative hybridization coordinate Z records this sector-resolved hybridization: its magnitude measures the local mixing strength, shown by the color scale on the band, while its phase retains the coherent phase information of the hybridization, indicated schematically by the small arrows along the texture.
